messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael was forty-nine when he finally walked into a therapist’s office, a year after retiring from the city council. He had served two terms, known for his steady voice in budget debates and his reluctance to attend community meet-and-greets. His wife, Diane, had been after him for months. “You flinch every time I touch you,” she said. “You haven’t slept through the night in years. Something’s wrong.” He knew she was right, but he couldn’t bring himself to explain why.

The trouble started in Afghanistan, during his second deployment. He was a logistics officer, not infantry, but that didn’t matter the day the convoy hit an IED. He remembered the blast — the pressure, the ringing, the smoke — but after that, the memory broke apart. He could piece together fragments: the medic’s hands on his arm, a soldier shouting, the taste of dust and copper. But the middle was gone, a blank that left him dizzy when he tried to fill it. When he recounted the event to Diane or to his VA doctor, he would lose his thread mid-sentence, stammer, and give up. The terror, though, never faded. Every time the memory surfaced — triggered by a car backfiring or a helicopter overhead — it hit him with the same visceral force, his heart hammering, his chest tight.

Back home, Michael began to see the world differently. The bombing had taught him that danger could be anywhere, and he became certain that he had to stay on guard at all times. He scanned crowds for suspicious packages, noted every exit in a room, and sat with his back to the wall at restaurants. His own body betrayed him: his palms would sweat, his muscles would tense, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline for no reason he could name. He came to believe that his body was his enemy, reacting as if the IED were still detonating. This sense of constant threat made it impossible to trust safety even when Diane assured him they were fine. At night, he lay awake, listening for footsteps, and when he finally fell asleep, a sudden sound would jolt him awake, gasping.

The threat itself spiraled back into his memory. The more hypervigilant he became, the more he noticed gaps in his recall — he would catch himself flinching at a touch and then wonder what he had been remembering, the fragments seeming to dissolve further. Sleep deprivation eroded his concentration, making the blank spots in his story even larger.

To cope, Michael developed strategies that he thought would keep him functional. He blasted loud music or talk radio whenever he was home alone, using the noise to drown out intrusive images. He constantly monitored his own thoughts, scanning for any sign that he was “losing it” — a flash of anger, a memory that came on too strong. And he avoided being touched by anyone: no handshakes at council events, no hugs from friends, no sudden pats on the back. When Diane reached for him in bed, he would stiffen and pull away.

These strategies, however, only made things worse. The sensory distraction kept him from sitting with his memories, so they never integrated; he remained stuck with the same incomplete, terror-laden fragments. His thought monitoring convinced him that something was wrong with his mind, reinforcing the belief that his body and brain were untrustworthy. Avoiding touch meant he never had a corrective experience — nobody’s gentle touch ever taught him that contact could be safe. Instead, any accidental brush from a constituent at a town hall sent his heart racing, and he would retreat into his office, certain the world was dangerous.

The cycle tightened. Because he could not trust his own memory, he felt more vulnerable, which deepened his hypervigilance. Because he was always on guard, his memory stayed fragmented and frightening. His negative appraisals — the world is dangerous, my body is against me — fed directly into his sense of threat, making the startle response quicker and the sleeplessness worse. In turn, every startle, every sleepless night, confirmed that he was right to see danger everywhere.

What finally brought Michael to the clinic was a moment at a council retirement party. A colleague clapped him on the back, and he spun around, fist raised, before he could stop himself. The room went quiet. Diane had tears in her eyes. He realized then that his strategies were failing him as a husband and as a public servant. He still cannot explain what happened in that convoy without losing the thread, and the terror is as fresh as ever. He is afraid that therapy will mean reliving it, but he is more afraid of losing Diane — and himself — to the silence he has built around the missing parts of his story.
